title: The Lighthouse Keepers Who Vanished: Flannan Isles, 1900
creator: Halden Archive
description:
In December 1900 three lighthouse keepers disappeared from a rock in the Outer Hebrides. What actually happened?

Sponsored by Cartograph: 15% off your first framed historical map at https://cartograph.co/halden

Sources: Northern Lighthouse Board records, the Moore and Muirhead reports.

sentences.t: On the twenty-sixth of December, 1900, a supply boat called the Hesperus pulled up to Eilean Mor, the biggest of the Flannan Isles.
It's a lump of rock about twenty miles west of the Outer Hebrides, and on top of it sits a lighthouse that had only been lit a year earlier.
Three keepers were supposed to be on it.
James Ducat, the principal keeper, Thomas Marshall, and an occasional keeper named Donald MacArthur.
Normally, when the relief boat showed up, someone would come down to the landing, wave, maybe help with the ropes.
This time, nobody came.
The relief keeper, a man named Joseph Moore, climbed the steps up to the station by himself.
The gate was closed, the door was closed, and inside, the clock on the wall had stopped.
The beds were unmade, the fire was cold, and two of the three sets of oilskins were gone.
Which tells you two of the men went out in bad weather gear, and one of them went out in just his regular clothes.
And that one detail is what's kept people arguing for a hundred and twenty-five years.

Okay, the logbook.
So, the version of this story you've probably heard says the log describes a terrible storm, with one keeper crying and another praying.
And then a final entry that just says, storm ended, sea calm, God is over all.
It's incredibly creepy, and it's almost certainly made up.
Those entries first show up decades later in a magazine story, and nobody has ever produced the actual pages.
What we do have is the official report from the superintendent, Robert Muirhead, who came out a few days after Moore.
And Muirhead found something much more ordinary, and honestly much sadder.
Down at the west landing, the railings were bent, a supply box that sat thirty-odd meters above the water had been torn open, and turf had been ripped off the cliff edge.
Something very big had hit that landing, and it hit it from very high up.
His theory was that two of the men went down to secure gear during a storm, and a huge wave came up the gully and took them.
And the third man, the one without his oilskins, maybe saw it from above and ran down to help.
Nobody knows for sure, and the sea never gave anything back.
Next week, we're going to look at the other big theory, and why I think it doesn't hold up.
